title: Polygraphia III: The cipher that pretends to be an artificial language
summary: The paper studies a cipher inspired by Trithemius’s Polygraphia III, in which invented word forms encode individual plaintext letters. Its randomized simulations reproduce some Voynich-like aggregate properties but miss others, and the author explicitly does not attribute the manuscript to Trithemius, whose work postdates it.
established: In the described P.III scheme, invented words are organized into columns: each word substitutes for a plaintext character, and related-looking word forms in a column may encode different characters. The paper contrasts intended sequential column use with the possibility of using one column repeatedly (section 2).
The reported random-column simulations use all 132 columns or a 10-column subset, compared with Takahashi Currier A and B and several historical-language texts (section 3).

Table 3 gives h1−h2 values of 1.10 for the large-column simulation and 1.67 for the small-column simulation, versus 1.68 for Currier A and 1.87 for B. Word entropy is 10.74 and 6.52 in those simulations versus 9.88 and 9.89 in A and B; the closer character result for the small table comes with a much lower word entropy.

The simulated type-length distribution does not match the manuscript’s approximately binomial profile; the paper also reports substantial dependence of adjacent similar-word and repetition counts on the number of columns (sections 3.2–3.3).

open.question: Can an independently specified, historically plausible column-selection procedure simultaneously reproduce the manuscript’s word entropy, character entropy and adjacent similarity without discarding reversible encipherment?
open.check: Freeze a documented selection procedure and codebook before evaluation, calibrate reversibility and positive-control recovery on separate plaintexts, and evaluate the joint metrics on held-out pages.

open.question: How effectively can replacement tables and plaintext be recovered from ciphertext generated by the P.III scheme?
open.check: Generate blinded planted-key controls across fixed table sizes and selection strategies, then measure held-out plaintext recovery and false-positive behavior at a published search budget.
